name: Mansa Musa
info: Mansa Musa (c. 1280 – c. 1337) was the ninth Mansa of the Mali Empire in West Africa, remembered for his wealth in gold, his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 and Timbuktu's growth as a centre of Islamic learning.

facts.born: c. 1280; the date is unknown, but he appears to have been a young man in 1324; of the Keita dynasty of Mali, a descendant of Abu Bakr, brother of Sunjata, though his parentage is disputed
facts.died: c. 1337; the date is uncertain: 1332 or earlier by some reckonings, 1337 regarded as most likely by Nehemia Levtzion; place and manner are not recorded
facts.role: Ninth Mansa (ruler) of the Mali Empire, from the early 1300s until his death
facts.known: his hajj to Mecca in 1324–1325; lavish gifts of gold in Cairo; bringing Gao and Timbuktu into the Mali Empire; recruiting scholars such as Abu Ishaq al-Sahili; building in Timbuktu, including part of Djinguereber Mosque; a lasting reputation for fabulous wealth

t: Musa ruled the Mali Empire at its territorial peak, when its wealth came from taxing and controlling the trade in salt and in gold from Bambuk and Bure.

His pilgrimage of 1324–1325, with an enormous entourage and a vast supply of gold, made him known across North Africa and the Middle East, and most of what is known of him comes from Arabic writers who recorded it.
Arabic authors praised his generosity and justice, while Mandé oral tradition gives him little space and some of its performers say he wasted Mali's wealth.
dyk: Musa encouraged the belief that his wealth was inexhaustible by spreading rumours that gold grew like a plant in his kingdom. On the way home from Mecca he nonetheless ran out of money and had to borrow from Egyptian merchants.
ev: Musa becomes Mansa of Mali under unclear circumstances; by his own account his predecessor never returned from an expedition into the Atlantic Ocean
On his way to Mecca he reaches the outskirts of Cairo in July, meets the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad and stays three months, giving and spending freely
He completes the hajj; on the return to Cairo many of his pilgrims die of cold, starvation or bandit raids, and he goes into debt to merchants
The kingdom of Mossi invades and conquers Timbuktu; Musa regains the city, builds a rampart and stone fort and stations a standing army there
According to Ibn Khaldun, he sends an envoy to congratulate Abu al-Hasan Ali on the conquest of Tlemcen, which took place in May of that year
Musa dies; the date is uncertain, and by other reckonings he died in 1332 or earlier

sections.early:
The date of Musa's birth is unknown. He appears to have been a young man in 1324, and his birth is placed around 1280. His personal name, Musa, is the name of Moses in Islam; mansa, "ruler" or "king" in Mandé, was the title of the rulers of the Mali Empire. In oral tradition and the Timbuktu Chronicles he is also Kanku Musa, "Musa, son of Kanku", after the Mandé custom of prefixing a mother's name, though it is unclear whether that genealogy is literal. The Tarikh al-fattash claims that he accidentally killed Kanku at some point before his pilgrimage.

His parentage is disputed. According to Djibril Tamsir Niane, his father was Faga Leye, son of Abu Bakr, a brother of Sunjata, the first mansa of Mali. Ibn Khaldun calls him Musa ibn Abu Bakr, which may mean a son or a descendant of Abu Bakr, and Ibn Battuta, who visited Mali under Musa's brother Sulayman, named his grandfather as Sariq Jata, perhaps another name for Sunjata. The historian Francois-Xavier Fauvelle has proposed that Musa was the son of Abu Bakr I, a grandson of Sunjata through his daughter, and that later attempts to erase a possibly illegitimate succession through the female line confused the sources.

The empire he was born into drew its wealth from the control and taxing of trade: salt from the north and, above all, gold panned and mined in Bambuk and Bure to the south. At his accession Mali consisted largely of the territory of the former Ghana Empire, which had become its vassal.
sections.rise:
Musa came to power in the early 1300s under unclear circumstances, as a young man, possibly in his early twenties. By his own account, given in Cairo, his predecessor as mansa, presumably Muhammad ibn Qu, launched two expeditions to explore the Atlantic Ocean, the first of 200 ships and the second of 2,000. The mansa led the second himself and appointed Musa as his deputy to rule until he returned. When he did not, Musa was crowned, and the succession passed from the descendants of Sunjata to those of his brother Abu Bakr. Some modern historians doubt this version and suggest that Musa may have deposed his predecessor and devised the story of the voyage to explain how he took power; several others have taken the possibility of such a voyage seriously.

Given the scale of his later pilgrimage, he probably spent much of his early reign preparing for it. The gold he carried probably represented years of accumulated tribute. The preparations are likely to have included raids to capture and enslave people from neighbouring lands, since his entourage included many thousands of slaves; the historian Michael Gomez estimates that Mali may have captured over 6,000 slaves a year for this purpose. Perhaps for this reason, his early reign was spent in continuous military conflict with neighbouring non-Muslim societies. In Cairo in 1324 Musa said that he had conquered 24 cities and their surrounding districts. When he left for Mecca he appointed his son Muhammad to rule in his absence.
sections.deeds:
Musa made the hajj between 1324 and 1325. Arabic chroniclers writing afterwards give widely varying figures for his caravan, which modern historians treat as rhetorical rather than statistical: upwards of 12,000 slaves, each said to have carried 1.8 kg of gold bars, and 80 camels each said to have carried between 23 and 136 kg of gold dust. He is said to have given gold to the poor and to the cities along his route. He reached the outskirts of Cairo in July 1324, camped for three days by the Pyramids of Giza and crossed the Nile on 19 July. The Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad expected him to prostrate himself; Musa at first refused, and when he did bow said he did so for God alone. The two rulers nevertheless exchanged gifts, and Musa left with the official caravan on 18 October. In Mecca he persuaded his men to back down when swords were drawn between Malian and Turkic pilgrims in the Masjid al-Haram.

He expanded Mali's borders, bringing in Gao and Timbuktu. The Tarikh al-Sudan says both cities submitted as he passed on his return; one account in Ibn Khaldun credits his general Saghmanja with conquering Gao, and another dates that conquest to Mansa Sakura. He sought closer ties with the Mamluk and Marinid sultanates and brought scholars to Mali, among them Maliki jurists and the Andalusi poet Abu Ishaq al-Sahili. Timbuktu became a centre of trade and Islamic scholarship; the University of Sankore was restaffed with jurists, astronomers and mathematicians, and his reign is associated with a portion of Djinguereber Mosque.
sections.opponents:
Musa's critics are found chiefly in Mandé oral tradition. The jeliw, or griots, say comparatively little of him, criticise him as unfaithful to tradition, and some regard him as having wasted Mali's wealth. Fauvelle suggests that hostility towards Musa's branch of the Keita dynasty would explain his relative absence from, or scathing treatment by, the oral histories.

The pilgrimage also ended badly. Travelling back from Mecca apart from the main caravan, many of the Malian pilgrims died of cold, starvation or bandit raids before reaching Suez. Musa ran out of money, resold much of what he had bought in Cairo and borrowed from merchants such as Siraj al-Din at a high rate of interest. Al-Umari and Ibn Khaldun state that the moneylenders were never repaid or only partly repaid; other sources disagree.

Later judgements of his wealth and works have been disputed as well. Al-Umari said that Musa's gifts lowered the value of a mithqal of gold in Egypt from 25 silver dirhams to less than 22 for at least twelve years. This has been described as having "wrecked" Egypt's economy, but the historian Warren Schultz argues that it was well within normal fluctuations. Hadrien Collet and other historians hold that his wealth cannot be calculated accurately, and conversions into modern money are regarded as methodologically unsound. J. O. Hunwick has shown that the only project firmly attributable to al-Sahili is a royal audience chamber, and modern scholarship regards the image of him as founder of West African mosque architecture as a historiographical myth.
sections.last:
In the years after the pilgrimage Timbuktu drew merchants from Hausaland, Egypt and other African kingdoms, and news of it reached southern Europe, where traders from Venice, Granada and Genoa added the city to their maps. In 1330 the kingdom of Mossi invaded and conquered Timbuktu. Musa quickly regained it, built a rampart and a stone fort, and placed a standing army there to protect it from future invaders.

The date of his death is uncertain. Counting back by Ibn Khaldun's reign lengths from the death of Mansa Suleyman in 1360, Musa would have died in 1332. Yet Ibn Khaldun also reports that Musa sent an envoy to congratulate Abu al-Hasan Ali on his conquest of Tlemcen, which took place in May 1337, and that by the time an envoy came in reply Musa had died and Suleyman was on the throne. Al-Umari, writing in approximately 1337, twelve years after the hajj, claimed that Musa returned to Mali intending to abdicate and go back to live in Mecca, but died before he could do so, which suggests a date even earlier than 1332. Nehemia Levtzion regarded 1337 as the most likely date, and other scholars have accepted it.

The succession is tangled with the same problem. It may have been Musa's son Maghan who congratulated Abu al-Hasan or received his envoy, and Ibn Khaldun may have confused Musa's brother Suleyman with Maghan. Alternatively, the four-year reign that Ibn Khaldun credits to Maghan may refer to his rule while Musa was away on the hajj, with only a brief reign in his own right before Suleyman.
sections.legacy:
Musa's reign is commonly regarded as Mali's golden age, though this may reflect its being the reign best recorded by Arabic sources rather than his necessarily being the wealthiest and most powerful mansa. The empire's territory was at its height under Musa and his brother Sulayman, covering the Sudan-Sahel region of West Africa. His palace has vanished, but the mosque and university of Timbuktu still stand.

In Mandé oral tradition some aspects of Musa appear to have passed into Fajigi, "father of hope", who is remembered as travelling to Mecca to retrieve the ceremonial objects called boliw and who combines Islam with traditional beliefs. The name Musa has become virtually synonymous with pilgrimage, so that other figures remembered as pilgrims are also called Musa. Arabic writers such as Ibn Battuta praised his generosity, virtue and intelligence, and Ibn Khaldun wrote that he "was an upright man and a great king, and tales of his justice are still told".

Abroad he became "a symbol of fabulous wealth". A tradition of showing a wealthy West African monarch on European maps runs from Angelino Dulcert's map of 1339 and the Catalan Atlas of 1375 to the Mansa Musa Map made by the Sicilian Jacopo Russo in 1525. Online articles in the 21st century have called him the richest person of all time, and Encyclopedia Britannica states that he is "widely considered to be the wealthiest person in history"; historians answer that the Arabic sources were probably expressing that he had more gold than they thought possible rather than giving an exact number.

summary: Mansa Musa ruled the Mali Empire at its greatest extent in the early 14th century. His pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324–1325 and his gifts of gold in Cairo made him famous in the Muslim world and on European maps, while Timbuktu grew as a centre of trade and learning. Much about his birth, accession and death remains uncertain.

notes: start 1280 and end 1337 are the article's lead dates (c. 1280 – c. 1337); the body says the birth date is unknown and the death date uncertain (1332, earlier than 1332, or 1337).
The saved article's 'Other sources' list is empty, so only three references could be copied, two of them primary sources cited through 'Levtzion & Hopkins 2000' (no full title given).
The article spells the brother's name both Sulayman and Suleyman; both spellings appear here as in the passages they come from. The editor may wish to unify.
The 1337 event (envoy to Abu al-Hasan) is Ibn Khaldun's report; the article notes it may have been Musa's son Maghan who sent or received the envoy.

The article's lead says a university was 'founded' in Timbuktu and the body says Sankore was 'restaffed'; I used 'restaffed'. The statement that Timbuktu was added to maps by traders from Venice, Granada and Genoa is as the article gives it.
'Gave gold to the poor', 'built a mosque every Friday' and the caravan figures are reported, not established; the mosque-every-Friday claim was left out.
The return disaster and debts are told under opponents (failures) rather than last, since they date to c. 1325.
Left out: the Tadmekka gold-refining finding, the copper trade, the Djenné-Djenno excavations, the 18 tons estimate.
